vascular_cognitive_impairment.summary: No disease-modifying therapy exists for vascular cognitive impairment; management is control of the vascular risk factors, secondary prevention matched to the mechanism, review of the anticholinergic burden, and treatment of coexisting Alzheimer pathology where biomarkers support it.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not choose one diagnosis when both are demonstrated — the treatment implications differ and both are needed
Do not stop anticoagulation because a single deep microbleed is present in a patient with atrial fibrillation and no falls
Do not omit vascular risk-factor treatment because the amnestic profile is 'typical Alzheimer'
Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications alongside a cholinesterase inhibitor
Do not attribute the decline to age or to thyroid disease on stable replacement
required_recommendations: Characterise the memory deficit as storage or retrieval type, because it determines which pathology leads
Read the MRI for both the atrophy grade and the vascular burden rather than reporting one of them
Obtain Alzheimer biomarkers where a vascular burden coexists with an amnestic profile, because the answer changes treatment
Exclude reversible causes, including thyroid disease on replacement
Name mixed disease explicitly rather than choosing between the two diagnoses
Review the anticoagulation indication against the microbleed burden and falls risk, and continue it where the balance favours it
Treat both the Alzheimer component and the vascular risk factors, and provide caregiver support

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG has no diagnostic role in vascular cognitive impairment; it belongs to the differential of a rapidly progressive or fluctuating course (Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease, non-convulsive status, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy), none of which is present here

A presynaptic dopaminergic study answers the Lewy-body question, not the vascular one, and there is no spontaneous parkinsonism, no fluctuating cognition with hallucinations and no REM sleep behaviour disorder
Cardiac sympathetic imaging is a test for dementia with Lewy bodies and for autonomic failure; it says nothing about cerebrovascular disease

An untargeted paraneoplastic or autoimmune-encephalitis battery in a chronic stepwise decline with a hypertensive imaging burden is the archetypal expensive miss; the indication for those assays is a subacute multidomain syndrome
The MRI already obtained answers everything a CT could and more: CT cannot show microbleeds or cortical superficial siderosis, so it cannot grade the vascular burden this diagnosis rests on
There is no embolic lesion pattern to explain: the burden here is small-vessel, and a structural cardioembolic source would not account for it
Prolonged rhythm monitoring is for an unexplained embolic infarct pattern; in pure small-vessel disease it changes nothing about the diagnosis or the treatment

accepted: Mixed Alzheimer and vascular dementia — biomarker-confirmed Alzheimer pathology with moderate cerebral small-vessel disease

differential.key_features: The amnestic profile, the atrophy and the biomarkers all support Alzheimer pathology, but a Fazekas 2 burden with two lacunes is a genuine second contributor that carries its own treatment implications, and calling it Alzheimer's disease alone would leave the vascular risk untreated
The amnesia is storage-type and unresponsive to cueing, the atrophy is Scheltens 3, and the biomarkers are positive; a Fazekas 2 burden cannot account for this profile
Four years of atrial fibrillation but no cortical or territorial infarct on MRI — the anticoagulation appears to have done its work
No fluctuation, hallucinations, spontaneous parkinsonism or dream enactment

key_clinical_evidence: Mixed disease is the commonest pathology of dementia in this age group, and it is a diagnosis rather than an inability to choose
Storage-type amnesia unresponsive to cueing with Scheltens 3 atrophy is the Alzheimer signature; a Fazekas 2 burden with lacunes cannot produce it
Biomarkers are worth obtaining precisely when a vascular burden coexists, because they determine whether a cholinesterase inhibitor is indicated
Four years of atrial fibrillation with no cortical infarct is evidence that anticoagulation has worked, and a single deep microbleed does not overturn the indication
Naming both components produces two management plans; naming one leaves half the disease untreated

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: There is no cortical or territorial infarct on MRI after four years of anticoagulated atrial fibrillation; the mechanism of this dementia is degenerative with a small-vessel contribution
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests a cardioembolic multi-infarct mechanism and directs the workup to an embolic source

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: One microbleed in a deep hypertensive distribution, with no lobar microbleeds, no siderosis and no falls, does not outweigh the stroke-prevention benefit of anticoagulation
red_herrings.intended_effect: Prompts withdrawal of anticoagulation in a patient with atrial fibrillation

clinical_assessment.impression: MoCA 18/30 with a dense storage-type amnesia that does not improve with cueing or recognition, together with executive and visuospatial impairment. The amnestic-led, gradually progressive profile is that of Alzheimer's disease; the executive component and the vascular risk profile raise the question of an additional vascular contribution, which the imaging and biomarkers must settle.

csf.interpretation: Positive Alzheimer biomarker profile: Abeta42 356 pg/mL, Abeta42/40 ratio 0.042 and phospho-tau 96 pg/mL. Amyloid and tau pathology are established. With a Fazekas 2 vascular burden and two lacunes also present, the diagnosis is mixed Alzheimer and vascular dementia rather than either alone.

labs.interpretation: TSH 1.4 mIU/L is normal on replacement, excluding hypothyroid cognitive impairment. LDL 98 mg/dL is above target. B12, folate, RPR and HIV normal or negative. No reversible cause is present.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Giovanna Rizzi is a 78-year-old retired midwife who attends with her husband. He describes four years of gradually worsening memory: she began by forgetting conversations and appointments, then started to lose objects and to repeat questions within minutes, and in the past year has become unable to cook meals she had made for fifty years or to manage her own medication. He is clear that the decline has been gradual throughout, with no abrupt steps he can date, and that memory has been the leading problem from the start rather than slowness or disorganisation. She stopped driving a year ago after two minor collisions in car parks. Her mother and two maternal aunts developed dementia in their seventies. She has had atrial fibrillation for four years, is anticoagulated, and has never had a clinical stroke. She has no hallucinations, no fluctuation in alertness, no dream enactment and no parkinsonian features. Her blood pressure has been in the 140-150 range and her thyroid replacement is stable.

neurological_exam.additional: Pulse irregularly irregular at 74. No frontal release signs. No parkinsonian features.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive. Extraocular movements full. Visual fields full. Face symmetric. Speech fluent with occasional word-finding pauses.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly cautious with slightly reduced step length; arm swing preserved. Tandem possible with corrections. No falls.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place and year; month and date incorrect. MoCA 18/30 with losses in trail-making, cube, clock, digit span, serial sevens, fluency (8 animals) and delayed recall (0/5 unaided, 1/5 with cueing, 2/5 on recognition). Repeats the same question three times during the consultation.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone. Strength 5/5 throughout. No drift.
